newsitem.title: USA: Clinton plans large U.S. farmland retirement.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plans large U.S. farmland retirement.

text.p: The Clinton administration expects to keep the maximum amount of land -- 36.4 million acres -- in the Conservation Reserve under new operating rules that will be released soon, budget documents said Thursday.

The future of the reserve is a major issue in the farm and environmental communities. Grain groups fear U.S. food output would suffer if too much land is enrolled, while conservationists want to make sure only fragile land is part of the programme.
Lawmakers like Senator Pat Roberts, a Kansas Republican, have campaigned to make sure the Great Plains maintains its large role in the programme.
Created in 1985, the reserve is the largest long-term U.S. land-retirement programme ever. It pays farmers an annual rent to hold fragile land out of production for 10 years.
This year was expected to bring major change to the reserve. Along with new operating rules, contracts on 24 million acres now in the reserve were due to expire this fall.

Budget documents said the reserve "is assumed to be gradually increased to 36.4 million acres by 2001." Agriculture Deprtment estimates say the reserve would dip to 30.3 million acres in fiscal 1998 before rebounding.

By comparison, the U.S. Feed Grains Council forecast early this week that enrollment would fall to 28.7 million acres in 1998-99 and rise steadily to 32 million acres in 2005. The council, a trade group, says strong demand and high prices for U.S. grain will encourage farmers to expand sowings.
"My concern is not the 36.4 million (acres) but what (type of land) is in that ... and what is the cost? And, what is the benefit, of course," said Maureen Hinckle of the National Audubon Society.
Ken Cook of the Environmental Working Group warned against reading too much into the acreage target. More important would be how the Agriculture Department decides which land to enroll.
"It's one of the biggest question marks in U.S. agriculture ... how the programme is going to evolve," Cook said.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman has said the reserve will be carefully managed to focus on highest results on soil erosion, water quality and wildlife habitat.

The National Grain and Feed Association said so much land potentially would be eligible for enrollment that U.S. grain production could be compromised. The reserve might end up unwisely throttling U.S. output, NGFA said in a recent letter to Glickman.
